BasePK: 3427494

Speech:
1.	Was the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development advised by way of a letter dated April 12, 1983 that, because of financial constraints, the Eskimo Dog Foundation was unable to continue its work of preservation and breeding the Canadian Eskimo dog which has attracted so much international interest over the past few years and that the Foundation plans to donate its stock of some 60 registered dogs to the government on May 31, 1983?
2.	What plans does the Government have for the dogs it will receive and will it continue the work initiated by the Foundation of preservation of this unique and endangered breed?

For each speech, return valid JSON with two fields:

1. `topic`: a short noun phrase, maximum 8 words, describing the main substantive topic.

- If no substantive topic can be identified, use "unclear".

- 0.25 = mostly substantive, with minor procedural formulae or partisan rhetoric.
- 0.50 = mixed substantive and procedural/partisan/formal content.
- 0.75 = mostly procedural, partisan attack, obstruction/delay, or formal intervention, with some substantive content.

BasePK: 3427548

Speech:
I want to advise the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) that I am concerned about the admissibility of the amendments. When I look at the motion that is before the House in the name of the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan), which refers to a loss of control over Crown corporations such as Air Canada, CN, etc., the amendment proposes to apply the same words-a loss of control over private corporations such as Eastern Provincial Airways, Canadian Pacific Limited and Power Corporation of Canada. Obviously, within the terms of the language of both the amendment and the motion, the motion itself indicates a loss of control over public corporations. The amendment, by the nature of its placement within the motion, refers to a loss of control over private corporations. I believe that may give some problem. Obviously, the Chair is going to suggest that debate continue while consideration is being given to the amendment. However, 1 believe, if I may assist the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), a more appropriate place for his amendment would be after the word "Maislin" within the main motion, ". . . with such private concerns as Maislin,. .then "and private corporations . . ." follows. I am not sure that it is an essential matter and I wonder whether the Hon. Member for Regina West, after reflection, might consider accepting a suggestion to put his amendment in that particular position rather than the one he has proposed?

BasePK: 3427615

Speech:
To fill the planes. It was losing $38 million but was in a position to cut its tariffs in the peak season in order to fill the planes when the private sector airline could not do it. In that same period the private sector airline lost its working capital. If it were not the subsidiary of a corporation as large as Canadian Pacific investments, it would not exist.
I have been suggesting in the House for some time now that if we were not able to cancel the debts of Canadian Pacific Airlines in the same way we cancel Air Canada's debt-if the equations were not in balance-there would be no way for the private sector airline to compete with a Government subsidized airline.
I speak of CPA because their head offices are in my region. I want to see that payroll survive as, I am sure, the Minister does as well. The factors must be balanced. It is easy for us in the House to cancel the debt of Air Canada. It is the only airline in North America that need not worry about having so much equipment backed up against the fence. It is the only airline that can survive while having so much equipment unused.
On the other hand, CP has one of the best records in the world in terms of air time on their equipment. They must make full use of their equipment because they cannot survive unless they implement every single productivity trick in the book in terms of productivity. This involves the management of capital, capital equipment and personnel. The personnel at Canadian Pacific have a different spirit because they realize the delicacy of their jobs.
I will say again to a very reasonable Minister of Transport-[DOT] as long as he does not bring in the Crow-that if this equation is not addressed I must come to the conclusion that it is a deliberate Government policy to peel the orange of Canadian Pacific Airlines with all that will do.

June 3, 1983
Supply
I can suggest what the Chief Executive Officer of Air Canada will do if the orange of Canadian Pacific Airlines is peeled. He will turn that very efficient national airline into an airline of box lunches. I remember from a conversation with him some years ago that the cost of proper service and the better treatment of passengers according to the standard that was being set by a competing airline was causing him to scratch his head in terms of the P&L. He questioned if he could get into this box lunch approach instead of the fancy service which is provided on the airlines. I agree with that in some respects but it is competition that causes good standard of service to be delivered.
My plea to the Minister is that he recognize this serious situation. While I have his attention let me say that I do not know how a company like Canadair with the problems it has can advertise in this manner. 1 do not know how they can do it or what purpose it serves.
While I am on the subject of Canadair, I remember back in 1979-1980 when the problem of the quality of the order book to justify the original investment was brought to my attention. This comes back to the problem of behaviour in that subgovernment and the need for accountability. At that time an order for 25 Challengers was laid on my desk. The person who gave that order in Europe did not have the wherewithal, the means or the intention to buy 25 aircraft. Yet those bookings were the justification for the Government's investment in the first place.
I would like to see Members of Parliament become far more knowledgeable and supported by sound research abilities in our accountability committees. I believe Members should have some expertise to enable them to examine the parameters of and justification for some of these investments. No matter which Government is in power it will be presented with Cabinet documents providing options on which decisions will have to be made. However, I believe that it is ultimately up to us as the elected directors of the shareholders of Canada to do a better job in that respect than is being done presently.
The issue surrounding the water bomber question troubles me. The thing I love about Canada and what I suppose has attracted so many people to this country is that one could come here with nothing. One could be born in poverty, and I believe that it is actually an advantage to be raised in this country with very little in the way of material possessions. People with little gain a burning hunger to want more. Therefore people learned to work, educate themselves, save money and take risks. They may get burnt but would come back again. That is what built this country. If there is no balance in the rule book or a measure of accountability and answerability by this Government's subsector, and it is allowed to run wild, I believe that that dream which energizes so many people will be lost.
With respect to the water bombers, is it fair that because there is a threat of a plant closing down in one city of Canada to subsidize a great fleet of equipment? What does that do to all the independent helicopter operators across the country who sit idle all winter with their equipment waiting to service the provincial needs for forest fires, the mining needs, the
exploration needs and other requirements? Each time a factor such as the water bomber proposal is put into the country's economy, what happens to the private sector that is waiting with its investment in a service? I am thinking in particular of a good operation at Pat Bay which has been carrying on business for years re-engining World War II equipment as water bombers. Is it now in or out of that field of endeavour? I would remind the Minister that even Bill Davis is flying a water bomber these days.
With respect to the accountability equation, for the Minister's benefit I am holding a series of reports from 1978 on. A colleague of his, a former President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State of Economic Development, was deeply involved in this package, as were other Members on his side and on this side. They were calling for an improvement [...truncated]

BasePK: 3427618

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great attention to the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington). I know he has many valuable ideas regarding accountability. Some of his ideas I would personally like to see implemented in this institution of Parliament.
The Hon. Member for Capilano talks a lot about subgovernment. There is no doubt there is a subgovernment that is becoming more and more powerful while the elected representatives of the people become less and less powerful. There is also in our system what I would now call the fetish of ministerial responsibiitv where Ministers are held accountable for everything within a vast array of departmental networks and Crown corporations. We all know there is no human being who can follow all of those activities and really be accountable for them.
Would the Hon. Member care to comment on the possibility of exchanging the theory and practice of ministerial responsibility for the greater accountability of this subgovernment, as he calls it quite rightly, to committees of Parliament?

BasePK: 3427639

Speech:
What do they want Parliament to do? Lie down and roll over? That is what they would like.
Regardless of the Prime Minister's opinion of Parliamentarians, Parliament will not do that unless, of course, the Government adopts the attitude which was adopted in Ghana when that new democracy modelled after Westminster was formed. The Government did not like the opposition there so it abolished it and threw half of them in jail. That is not going to happen here.
The sheer length and complexity of the Government business is another element in this Government's continuing contempt for the institution, its traditions and clear and central position in preserving the freedom of Canadians. No
Government has ever before in our history been so interventionist. This Government's centralizing policies have imposed upon Parliament a nearly insupportable burden of legislative quackery and parliamentary fiddle-faddle that no Parliament should have to put up with.
Because of this Government's inertia and incurable propensity to cover its tracks, we have had to take time out to extract the painful and distressing story of the clandestine arrangement between a former Minister and his colleagues in the Gillespie affair. We have been seized with the regrettable and sorry affair of another former Liberal Minister now before the courts. We have had the issue of a chairman of a major Crown corporation under investigation. In each of these areas the Government has thrown a smokescreen around Parliament's right to know. The official cover-up has gone into play.
In spite of the whiff of corruption emanating from that side, we are put off with the excuse that the matter is under investigation. These exercises in insider corruption within the Liberal Party do not serve to enhance the image of the Liberal Party.
There are Members on that side who are just as scandalized and just as disillusioned as we are in these matters. There are honest Members on the Government side. They are decent, hardworking Parliamentarians with an abiding respect for the institution and its traditions who are shocked and put off most strongly at the way in which Parliament is being degraded under this Government. They are concerned, as we are, at the parallel Government which is the personal creation of the Prime Minister, a caricature of Government, run by his flunkies which the Prime Minister has instituted to carry out his personal ideology. It is referred to by the Auditor General as a Government within a Government. The spidery network of Crown corporations and agencies, holding companies and quasi private corporations operated from the Prime Minister's office constitute a threat to the freedom of this country. What he cannot do by the front door, he is trying to do by the back door.
Parliament stands in the way of the socialization of this nation against the popular will. Therefore he is attempting to bring it about extra-legally and extra-curricularly by using public funds and the efforts of men who are sworn to carry out the wishes of the Prime Minister. This man has more court favourites than Louis XIV and each one has his own private little kingdom to operate at the taxpayers' expense.
It is true that they go through the motions of bringing these matters to Parliament, but well after the fact. What will the House of Commons do with 1,400 gas stations? Perhaps they will serve as a place of employment for Grit flunkies after the next election.
Continuing contempt, disregard, neglect and abuse of Parliament has been the hallmark of this Government. From the buffoonery of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in front of the TV cameras with his budget papers to the backing and filling of the Prime Minister in delicate international matters of primary concern to Canadians, Parliament has been told to take a back seat.
June 6, 1983

It has been made clear to this House, elected to serve and to represent Canadians in the same way as the Prime Minister was elected, that we have all been red circled. This House has been kept sitting here longer than any Parliament in the history of this country, including the "long Parliament, of Charles I. We have not had a Throne Speech in nearly four years. What does that mean? It means there has been no blueprint of Government plans, no blueprint of Government intentions, so that Parliament has been kept deliberately in the dark. I would venture to suggest, Sir, that if Parliament is in the dark it is not more so than the Cabinet itself, whose members are usually the last to know about the Prime Minister's intentions.
Parliament has been inhibited in carrying out its functions. This House has been prevented from acting on major national issues, such as unemployment, high interest rates, bankruptcies and the sliding of the economy down the slippery slope of recession simply because this Government has removed its expenditures from the control of Parliament. As a result, Canadians everywhere have suffered. They have been subject to policies of economic attrition. They have been made to pay in lost jobs, lost income, higher taxes for the inefficiencies of an arrogant Government wrapped in a cloak of its own isolation. We are now in the clearly unconstitutional position of going into the fourth year of this Parliament without a new session, another indication of the Government's contempt for those traditions and laws which have made parliamentary democracy the envy of the world.
Only Parliament stands in the way of the Prime Minister's attempt to create a kind of corporatist state in this country. In order to do this, it is necessary for him to break or to bypass the power of the House of Commons, weakened though it may be. He has been working very hard at doing so-

BasePK: 3427664

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, how much time do I have left? There is no way that 1 could adequately answer the Hon. Member as he deserves to be answered in the short time remaining. The fact is that as short as it was when we were in office for that seven months, it was our Secretary of State for External Affairs who was part of a government which brought accord to the two-track policy that is now being followed by the Government. Our policy on Cruise testing is known. It is succinct and it is public, and the Hon. Member knows that.
MO)
Since his coming into this House, I have noticed that he is prone to twisting, distorting and changing colour in order to suit the public opinion of the day. That Hon. Member's opinion cannot be accepted on any matter. All he does is twist, ride and distort for the purpose of pushing the so-called socialist position on anything: always grandstanding, like the Member in front of him. He is always attempting to grab an issue and then be very annoyed when he cannot do so.
That is understandable because (a) they are Members of the New Democratic Party; therefore, that explains a lot; and (b), they are in deep trouble in this country so they grab at anything they think will lift them up by their bootstraps, if they can see a way of doing it. They will grab on to anyone's coat tail. It does not matter whose coat tail it is, as long as they think it will give them a lift in the public opinion polls.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, just one point. One simply has to read and understand. The Hon. Member is talking about a vote after closure that took place merely to implement Standing Order 75a, b and c. That is absolutely not what I was talking about and that is absolutely not what his interim leader was talking about in his speech. We were talking about Opposition days, the Business of Supply. That is the reform and those are the rules to which I was referring and to which his leader was referring when I quoted Hansard and the Journals.
I would seek unanimous consent to table the proper extract from Commons Debates and the House of Commons Journals that very clearly demonstrate that in fact the Business of Supply, the Opposition days, were adopted unanimously by this House of Commons. I hope this consent will not be denied.

BasePK: 3427731

Speech:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Hamilton West (Mr. Hudecki) chided those Members of the Progressive Conservative Party who are Members of the House of Commons, and who are out seeking the leadership of the Party. I should like to suggest that they are doing a service to their country at the present time by letting their names stand for leadership of the Party. All of us in the House know that the next leader of the Conservative Party will be the Prime Minister of the country.

that Bill C-584, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (capital punishment), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He Said: Mr. Speaker, we are now at second reading of bill C-584, which is an Act to amend the Criminal Code to reinstate capital punishment for cases of premeditated first degree murder. We are discussing the subject today after a very long and sustained effort on the part of the Official Opposition, the Progressive Conservative Party, to have the serious question of capital punishment referred to committee and to allow a free vote in the House of Commons. I am attempting to satisfy the majority of my constituents who wish the Government to review the possibility of a return to capital punishment for premeditated first degree murder.
On December 15, 1980, as reported on page 5742 of Hansard, I asked the Government House Leader to allow one of the many Private Members' Bills dealing with capital punishment to come to a vote. I subsequently introduced this Private Members' Bill, Bill C-584, which received first reading on
Capital Punishment
May 2, 1980. I hoped then, as I do now, that the Bill would come up for debate during this session of the Thirty-second Parliament. Again, on January 27, 1981, as reported on page 6589 of Hansard, I rose under Standing Order 43, asking to refer the subject of capital punishment to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
On June 11, 1981, the Progressive Conservative Party managed to arrange an Opposition day in which I had the opportunity to present the motion which appears on page 10504 of Hansard once again to refer the question of the reintroduction of capital punishment as the penalty for some classes of murder to the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. Bill C-584, which has been on the Order Paper for four years, would effectively reimpose the death sentence in cases of first degree murder.
The decision to bring this matter to the attention of the House of Commons is not only representative of an enlightened leadership, but more significantly reaffirms the sense of responsibility towards the electorate which is shared by all Hon. Members of the Progressive Conservative Party.
In a poll conducted in the riding of Peterborough in 1981, 87.2 per cent of persons polled favoured a return to capital punishment for premeditated first degree murder. On a national level in 1982, a poll carried out by the Ottawa Citizen revealed that nearly three-quarters of the Canadian population want the death penalty restored and, even more, support a referendum on the question. The surveys accurately reflect the desire of a strong majority of all Members of Parliament to have a free vote on the question of capital punishment in order to fulfil their obligations and responsibilities to their constituents. I hope that this Bill, C-584, an Act to amend the Criminal Code, will be read a second time today and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, no, I do not. That was the point I made in my speech. Both as a New Democrat and as one who had the opportunity to study this issue in the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure, I have stated there is not enough accountability of Crown corporations to Government and I am concerned about the many quasi-government agencies that are proliferating and which need to be made accountable to this Parliament. We do not disagree on the need for more accountability. Where we disagree is on whether we are going to use that lack of accountability which exists to attack the existence of these instruments of public policy on principle, or whether we are going to make them accountable and thereby make them better instruments of public policy. Our second disagreement is whether we are going to make private power in this country as accountable to the common good as the Hon. Member and I want to make public power. That is where we disagree.

Let us not kid ourselves. When private corporations suffer losses, somebody picks up the cost of those losses. People either pick up these losses as taxpayers then they are Crown corporations, or pick them up as consumers if it is a private corporation. When private corporations suffer a loss, they do not assume that they cannot pass on that loss through the marketplace. It works its way into the marketplace. Let us not be naive about the way the marketplace works.

Mr. Speaker, to mark the patriation of the Canadian Charter the Government of the United Kingdom gave to Canada, on October 1, 1983, facsimilies of the major British documents respecting Canada's constitutional development, including the Royal Proclamation of 1763; the Quebec Act, 1774; the Constitutional Act, 1791; the Union Act, 1840; and the British North America Act, 1867. At the same time, the British Foreign Secretary, Francis Pym, also presented a special copy of the Canada Act 1982, produced on parchment.
The Speaker of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Commons decided that these documents of Canada's constitutional development should be put on display in the Hall of Honour so that thousands of Canadians who visit Parliament each year might be able to gain an even greater understanding of various stages in the evolution of Canada as a sovereign state.
They also decided that the edict creating the Sovereign Council of Quebec, 1663, which established New France as a royal Province and made provision for civil Government, should figure in the display. That original document is on loan from the Archives of France until September 5, 1983. The collection of documents of Canada's constitutional development also includes the proclamation of the Constitution Act, 1982, signed by Queen Elizabeth II. This document completed Canada's evolution as a fully sovereign state.
The collection of constitutional documents is complemented by a display of three proclamations establishing Canada's symbol of sovereignty: The Royal Proclamation of the Coat of Arms of Canada, 1921; the Proclamation of the Canadian Flag, 1965; and the Proclamation of the National Anthem, "O, Canada", 1980.
The number of documents to be included in such an exhibition is inevitably limited. The main exhibit deals only with the principle documents respecting Canada's constitutional development leading to full sovereignty, and the complementary exhibition deals only with the Canadian symbols of sovereignty. The exhibition of documents does not seek to deal with every aspect of Canada's constitutional and political evolution. For this reason, it was decided that another exhibition dealing with other aspects should be organized by the Public Archives.
I might say at this time that the Public Archives removed this document from the showcase because a signature on the document was being raised by the light reflecting in the
showcase.
It should be noted that the exhibition in the Hall of Honour includes The Proclamation of the Constitution Act, 1982, which brought into force that Act which includes the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. However, the Constitution Act, 1982, itself is not included in the display.

The collection of constitutional documents does not include the many historic statutes of the Parliament of Canada that are of great significance for the people of Canada, such as the Official Languages Act of 1969, or indeed the Canadian Citizenship Act of 1947 or, for that matter, the Canadian Bill of Rights of 1960. The exclusion of such documents does not reflect in any way on their importance for Canadians.

June 17, 1983
Electoral Boundaries
I want to stress at the outset that many of the things said to the Commission were said by representatives of all three political Parties and because of historical community interests and traditions in Saskatchewan. The point that really puzzled a lot of us in Saskatchewan is that the Boundaries Commission did not make very much use at all of the plus or minus 25 per cent rule. They drew arbitrary lines in many cases for our 14 Saskatchewan constituencies. They did not deviate from an average. For example, the least populous riding as recommended by them, to be called Regina-Lumsden, has a population of 67,183. The most populous riding is called Saskatoon-Dun-durn, which is primarily city but also partly rural, with a population of 71,432. So of the 14 ridings in Saskatchewan the difference between the least and the most populous will be 4,549 people. Mr. Speaker, I do not think that is good enough.
1 have had a chance to look at Boundary Commission reports from other Provinces and I notice that in many other Provinces the Commission has, in my opinion, more wisely interpreted the Act by making sure that the deviation is greater for sparsely populated and remote areas. The population will be larger for the urban centres. This was not done in Saskatchewan where a lot of the boundaries are very arbitrary. It is almost as if they took a calculator and divided our population into 14, then took a ruler and put it on the provincial census map and drew 14 areas. 1 do not think that is good enough. We should go back to the drawing board in Saskatchewan and come up with a map that the people of our Province want, one that will reflect the reality, the community interests, the history and traditions of Saskatchewan in a way which has been done many times in the past, and in other Provinces by Boundaries Commissions in the last few months.
To be specific, Mr. Speaker, the Commission ignored some of the guiding principles in planning redistribution, mainly the recognition of a community of interest. I can go over a number of these, and the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain could do the same thing, where that community of interests was often ignored by the Boundaries Commission. They wanted to have a more exact population figure in each riding, ignoring many times the community of interests.
The second principle they often ignored was the need to follow geographical patterns and boundaries. There is an excellent example of that in that part of the Province represented by myself and the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, namely the Qu'Appelle River Valley. The Qu'Appelle River is a natural geographical boundary and a natural community boundary. It is a natural boundary in so many ways historically in our Province yet that was ignored. In addition, the Commission did not agree to make as few changes as possible to establish ridings. That is spelled out in Subsection 13(b), Subsection 13(c)(1) and Subsection 13(c)(2) of the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act and is included in the terms of reference of the Commission. They did not follow the principle of community interests, geographical patterns and that of making as few changes as possible.

In the case of most other Acts where we have limits per customer, the Government and the Department of Agriculture have recognized legal partnerships and coop farms. But that is not the case with the Farm Improvement Loans Act. The limit is $100,000 regardless of a legal partnership or a co-op farm. A co-op farm may have anywhere up to a dozen members, and it may have a great need of a broad range of capital. However, the Farm Improvement Loans Act will allow them to borrow only up to $100,000, the same as an individual operator. I think that is something the Minister should keep in mind. Perhaps he could draw it to the attention of his officials so that when he or a future Minister brings the Farm Improvement Loans Act before the House another time the needs of co-op farmers could be dealt with as well.
We note the good experience with the Farm Improvement Loans Act since its inception in 1945 or 1946. It provided loans to farmers which assisted in the recovery of the economy after the Second World War. It put the machinery manufacturing sector on its feet, because it was basically farm improvement loans that went to farm machinery, and the two programs, development of the farm machinery industry and the provisions of credit, work very well together. In fact, until 1965, 100 per cent of the intermediate term loans which farmers took out were under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Until that time the rate was fixed at 5 per cent. After

1965, there were some changes to the Bank Act which permitted the banks to get back into the mortgage field, an area they had not been in for a long time. We can see the private banking system has moved into that particular field of credit in a fairly big way, thanks to the experience they got under the Farm Improvement Loans Act between 1946 and 1965.

Upon moving the previous question, the fact that the time limits as set out in the various Standing Orders apply means that you must go back to the beginning and apply them to the question that is before the House. The debate does not continue in the same way that it would if the motion were a motion of substance.
This is one of three potential closure motions or closure of debate motions. You can have a straight closure motion which would be subject to certain rules of debate; you can have a time allocation motion which is subject to certain rules of debate; and you can have this motion on the previous question which is subject to certain rules of debate. The rules of debate in the two previous situations are set out clearly in the Standing Orders. The rules for this motion are set out equally clearly in the Standing Orders inasmuch as the time limits for all other debates become applicable to this debate when it is moved to deal with the subject being dealt with under one of the Standing Orders in the House of Commons for debating purposes.
If the Government had moved closure, then the time limits are clearly set out as to the length of time debate would be permitted on that particular motion. The end result would be a vote on the bill. If the Government were to move time allocation, the length of time permitted is clearly set out and at the end the vote would be taken and a disposition of the Bill made at that stage. In this case it says that whatever Standing Order is applicable-and in this case we are talking about second reading stage-the time limits under the Standing Order become the time limits applicable for the motion to move the previous question.
I suggest, therefore, that at the time the motion is put the time limits become applicable based on the way they are written in the Standing Orders. In the Standing Orders the time limits are, one, that the Leader of the Opposition and the Leader of the Government have indefinite time; and two, that Members speaking in the first eight hours of the debate have 20 minutes and thereafter Members speaking beyond that point have ten minutes each. I suggest now that that is the Standing Order in terms of time limits that we are working under and that we should begin by accepting that the Leader of the Government and the Leader of the Official Opposition have unlimited time; that any Member during the first eight hours of debate has 20 minutes; and any Member speaking thereafter is permitted ten minutes. I would urge upon you

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to rise and speak on Bill C-155. I would like to make a few comments on closure and then indicate how I personally feel about the Bill before the House. When I first came here as a Member of Parliament, I felt very strongly that I could represent the people of my constituency with honour, integrity and a sense of feeling which is only gained from living in a constituency or in a particular area. Basically I thought all Hon. Members of Parliament would sit with open ears during debates and allow the exchange of ideas to take place so that Opposition Members could play their role by modifying bad legislation. In the parliamentary system which I understood, we in the House of Commons, as Members representing all of Canada, would reach a solution that would be palatable to every part of the country. Instead I found much to my dismay and sorrow that every time a piece of bad legislation came before the House or a piece of legislation with which some Members disagreed, the Government moved in with closure or time allocation which is another form of closure. It is not a place for debate; it is not a place in which to exchange ideas.
I doubt whether Hon. Members sitting on the Liberal backbenches really understand what the Crow rate is all about or what Bill C-155 does. For example, let me indicate what

June 20, 1983
Western Grain Transportation Act
exists right now as a statutory freight rate. The Crowsnest Pass Agreement was signed in 1897, nearly 100 years ago. CPR agreed to reduce rates for transporting grain and flour from western Canada to the Lakehead to five cents per ton mile. The rate became statutory in 1925 when it was incorporated in the Railway Act. Subsequently it was extended in later years to include Vancouver, Prince Rupert and Churchill and was broadened to include certain oilseeds and semi-processed grain products. That is what farmers in western Canada understood, and it has become part of the very social fabric of western Canada.
Now the Government virtually proposes to transfer $1 billion from the pockets of western Canadian farmers directly to the railways. That is exactly what is happening. The total revenue from farm commodities, grain from western Canada, is $6 billion. The Government is proposing to take $1 billion of that $6 billion and transfer it directly to the railways. It will not come from Government coffers; it will come directly out of the pockets of farmers in small communities in my riding and in every other western grain producing area.
It is an attack on the social fabric of western Canada. I am talking about the very small communities on the Prairies, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The very existence of places like Rochester is threatened. When you threaten the farmer, you kill the family farm. When you do that, you kill the very small communities such as Kinsella, Smith and other places Members have not even heard of. I repeat, they are the very social fabric of western Canada.
The Government has come in with Bill C-155. I outlined what the statutory Crow rate was all about. It is very simple, five cents a tonne mile. That was the transportation cost. What will the farmer pay now? I want to quote directly from the Bill. I say to Members opposite, for God's sake, read the Bill and see if you can understand it. I know you cannot. I quote the annual rate scale, Clause 35 on page 16. This tells the farmer how much he will pay in freight rates to ship his grain from western Canada to market. I quote:

Mr. Speaker, it is with no great pleasure that I rise tonight to speak at the end of the debate on Bill C-155.
This Bill does three things. It does away with the historic Crow rate, which is a right that has existed for Canadian farmers since 1897, a right which existed to attract people into parts of this country which were far from cheap ocean transport, without a great deal going for them in terms of climate.
As well this Bill has some proposals to improve the transportation system of this country, which I do not believe anyone is arguing about. There were some arguments put forward by some Hon, Members of my Party to point out better ways of spending the same amount of money; ways which would retain more control of the CPR and CNR and work toward the good of the people of Canada, ways which would get more "bang for the bucks", so to speak.
The third part of the Bill which is before us deals with the Dominion coal lands, a block of coal which has a current value of some $480 billion.
As the agricultural spokesperson for my Party, I considered at this stage of the debate of doing a thorough analysis-and I have the notes here-of what this kind of proposal does to farmers in western Canada, eastern Canada and in central Canada. It forces grain producers to give up some privileges to livestock producers in the way that it shifts production of livestock from one corner of the country to another in a vain attempt to give the impression that there is some economic development going on because of this policy. However, I have decided to use what time remains to me, Mr. Speaker, not to talk about what this policy does to the farmers of this country, but what it does to us all as Canadians.
Since this is the principal stage of debate where we should speak about principles I believe it is time to take a few moments to reflect on what the railway and transportation policy has attempted to do in this country. We have a kind of geography from which it is very nearly impossible to carve a country, Mr. Speaker. This was not a place where you would look at a map, understand the geography and decide that this is where a country should be. It makes absolutely no sense, geographically, economically or politically to have a country where we have this country of ours, Canada. It is held together because we are a stubborn race which insists on imposing East-West guidelines, East-West transportation and East-West communications, in spite of a more natural tendency for trade, communication and our social activities to go North-South.
What this proposal does is cut one of the fibres which holds this country together. It is a policy which was used to populate the West, the Prairies. It is a policy which we are now watching this Government abandon. It is an important move, Mr. Speaker, because it says to the people of Canada that a promise is no longer a promise and a deal is no longer a deal. It is killing the trust which has to exist if this country is going to continue as a country. It is taking away the one basic policy
which held western Canada together, which created an incentive for people to go and populate that area. What is happening is very similar to what would happen if some Government someday-God help us from such a Government-came along and said, "We have done all the economic studies. Bilingualism costs the country so many millions of dollars, so let us do away with bilingualism". The reasoning and logic is very similar here. The Government has brought in some economic thinkers who do not understand what makes the country tick, what holds it together, why it exists. It has looked at a very narrow item, has decided it is costly and therefore it should go. It has ignored what that does to the other minorities which exist in this country, not only Francophone minorities, but the Indian people who also had deals which were supposed to last into perpetuity, as long as the rivers shall flow and the grass shall grow. Here we are taking a proposition that was to last into perpetuity and the Government is saying, "We do not like it, we will break it and not pay any attention to that part of the country. We will give up on the East-West ties that bind this country together and introduce a policy the economics of which will force us to trade in a more North-South pattern". If this policy is implemented, transportation from western Canada will no longer have an economic reason to go through the St. Lawrence Seaway, it will go south to the Mississippi River system. It will take away jobs from the people of the central part of the country where they are now, and there is no way this country can survive such a policy.
This Bill should not pass second reading tonight. It needs more time. Therefore, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper):
That this House do now adjourn.

The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce set up the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board, or CIRB, to try to find means of increasing production and reducing costs to promote exports in so-called soft traditional sectors, such as the textile industry.
In addition, I think it is about time we developed new products in Canada, because all our young people are looking to microprocessors and high technology. The technological revolution may be just another phrase for us, but it is a reality in other countries. It is therefore important for a Department to be able to coordinate such activities. In the past, development meant research centres under the jurisdiction of other Departments than that of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and it was the responsibility of External Affairs to find new markets, but there had never been an economically-oriented Department working in very close co-operation with businessmen and businesswomen and able to point the way to new markets and new opportunities. All these activities will now be regrouped under three Departments: External Affairs, Regional Industrial Expansion and the Department which will be responsible for marketing. That is what we had to do, and under this legislation, I think that we shall have to see to it that there will be a single government agency in the various regions. I think this is an excellent piece of legislation, to the extent that it will bring us closer to the people and that we will not forever have to give other departments the information required to enable the people to act knowledgeably and responsibly. In addition, Madam Speaker, other duties of the Department include, and I quote:
(e) provide support services for industrial and trade development, including information, import analysis and traffic services-
Everyone will admit that the last consideration is of major importance to the country, the question of traffic services. Most of the time we do experience difficulties due to the vastness of our country and the lack of modern railway facilities. Besides, let us admit it, the high cost of transportation is often the only thing which prevents our merchants, businessmen and businesswomen from moving throughout the country to sell their goods-prohibitive transportation costs. The question of traffic services is basic in this Bill and we will have to make sure that it is more than pious wishes, that it becomes a reality so that we will be able to transport our own products from the Atlantic to the Pacific and, increasingly, from the Arctic to our southern borders. Afterwards we will have to make sure that with outstanding transporters such as Air Canada and CP Air we will take our goods to Europe. There are markets but we must look beyond North America. Granted, the United States remain our main trading partner, but we must seek new outlets in China and Japan because our country is blessed with natural resources. Japan, with her huge population, must protect every single tree which grows on her islands. Europeans are now looking for lumber producing countries. Canada is a country which can meet those needs, but we must process our lumber right here. Transportation should not however be an obstacle to our trade, but it is now one of of our
major difficulties. By combining the Department of External Affairs with the former Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, I think we have found a major lever to ensure Canada's economic recovery and diversification.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I should like to say that we will need more that economic recovery programs. We will be successful if all Canadians, men and women alike, are truly motivated not only politically, but individually and personally. I am convinced that we will have a few false starts at the beginning, because the whole apparatus will have to be put to the test, and that is to be expected. A number of public servants will be frustrated because many of them do have soft jobs. We are here to serve the public, find new formulas and make sure that we do not fall prey to a kind of lethargic sleep. This Bill will shake up some people, but that is our job and it is important that we do it well. Knowing as I do the new Leader of the Opposition, I am almost certain that he will be tempted to repeat word for word what I have just said. The major hazard facing the Leader of the Opposition-I do know him well

is that he is a good Liberal. I have always thought that he was a Liberal who had lost his way, so those who are more conservative that progressive should be on their toes! To conclude my remarks, Madam Speaker, I will say that this legislation is welcome. Like any Hon. Member on both sides of the House, I have a few legitimate reservations. But let us give a chance to the department before destroying it and let us wait and see what the results are. In addition, I am convinced that these provisions will benefit all Canadians. Nothing prevents us from reviewing the new legislation every year, for it is wrong to make changes in our laws only every 15 years. It is about time as well that the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce stop patronizing, leaving unimportant matters to small regions, and that we strike together, to achieve a really balanced development of our economy.

Evidence shall be excluded if it was obtained under such circumstances that its use in the proceedings would tend to bring the administration of justice into disrepute.
In 1975 the Law Reform Commission of Canada proposed an evidence code in its first report to Parliament. In that report the Commission advocated that a judge should have a power to exclude evidence in certain circumstances. Two provisions of that code are important to us in our consideration of the motion today. Section 15 of the proposed evidence code is identical to the recommendation contained in the report of the MacDonald Commission and in the motion brought before the House today. Accordingly, I need not read it now.
in Section 16 of its proposed evidence code, the Law Reform Commission recommended a specific provision concerning the admissibility of statements, and that provision reads as follows:
A statement made by the accused to a person in authority is inadmissible if tendered by the prosecution in a criminal proceeding, unless the judge is satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the statement was not made under circumstances (including the presence of threats or promises) that were likely to render the statement unreliable, or unless the accused personally or through his counsel agrees to its admission.
Nothing in this section affects the admissibility of evidence other than a statement of the accused, including evidence of any fact discovered as a result of such statement or that such facts were discovered as a result of the statement.
The legal profession in Canada did not greet the report prepared by the Law Reform Commission of Canada with much enthusiasm. As a result, the Law Reform Commission of Ontario turned its attention to the law of evidence, and subsequently published a report in 1976. In that report the Ontario Commission also recommended that a judge should have the discretion to exclude evidence is it was obtained illegally and its admission would be unfair to the opposing party, or if evidence was obtained by methods that are repugnant to the fair administration of justice. The latter part of this recommendation was expressly designed to combat what the Law Reform Commission of Ontario perceived as bad policy in the decision given by the Supreme Court of Canada in Regina v. Wray. I think this case has been referred to by all Hon. Members who have spoken on this matter.
Then in 1981, the MacDonald Commission, as it was popularly known, recommended that a legislative provision be enacted in terms identical to those proposed in Section 15 of the evidence code of the Law Reform Commission of Canada. In its report, the MacDonald Commission made a brief survey of law as it stands in Canada and in other jurisdictions, as well as a summary of arguments for and against the discretion to exclude illegally obtained evidence. The Commission expressed its support for a discretion to exclude in Clause 64 which reads as follows:
In our view, the law of Canada should, like that of Scotland and Australia, give the trial judge a discretion to exclude illegally and unfairly obtained evidence. It will be noted that we do not propose the adoption of the American rule requiring the absolute exclusion of all illegally obtained evidence. The Canadian rule should be discretionary rather than absolute, because:

An absolute rule fails to distinguish between a minor case such as shoplifting, and a grave case such as murder. Any rule that fails to discriminate between those different factual circumstances is too blunt an instrument to achieve any of its objectives, such as the preservation of judicial integrity and the deterrence of improper or illegal police conduct.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to make a statement against statements. Since January, when we adopted new rules, I believe that there has been a great undercutting of Members of Parliament because we now cannot put motions which will cause action to be taken over the words we say in the House. So far, they have been favouring some policies that I think are detrimental to Canadian people, specifically the so-called cruel and harsh restraint policies of Premier Bill Bennett in British Columbia which they have supported under the table. Those things will be debated in the future, but let me say something about this particular Bill. Let me speak about the problem with this particular Bill as I see it. My real concern is with the second part of this Bill, the consolidation of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the DREE Department or the Regional Economic Expansion
September 12, 1983

Department. What I think it means, Mr. Speaker, is that what the Bill will do, in fact, is make Industry, Trade and Commerce a major Government Department responsible for all of the internal business dealings in Canada, to put it broadly, whether large or small business, and the Department of External Affairs will deal with foreign trade as well as foreign matters of state that do not concern trade. I will point out later some of the problems that this will create, but in terms of regional development, what does this Bill mean?
We all want regional development in Canada. At least those of us from the West do. The Hon. Member who last spoke put it very well when he spoke about the need for having development in the smaller towns of Canada and the need to move away from central Canada and get some industrial development in other parts of Canada. In a long and narrow country like Canada, that need has been a consistent problem.
As I understand it, the way this Bill works is that DREE as a Department will be gone and Industry, Trade and Commerce will have project directors in each Province who will assess the regions and the projects and will report to a group in Ottawa called MSERD. It sounds a bit absurd, but it means the Minstry of State for Economic and Regional Development, or MSERD, as only those in Ottawa can say. The idea is that this will plug the regions into a high level of Cabinet and the employment Minister, I think, will then go directly to the central inner Cabinet with these regional concerns. Now that sounds good on paper. That sounds like the way regional development should be created, but there are some concerns. I found out about these concerns specifically last weekend when the NDP caucus held its retreat in Nova Scotia. The concerns were that if the Department of Regional Economic Expansion were abolished-a department created specifically to meet regional needs-and regional Development was put into the larger Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, perhaps some of the principles of regional concern will be forgotten. Perhaps they will not receive as high a priority as if there were a separate Department. That is what Alexa McDonough, the Leader of the NDP in Nova Scotia and other people there, told us. I have heard Members of the House say that in pretty well the same language, today.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, I think we all appreciate the concern of the Hon. Member for

September 14, 1983
Cruelty to Animals
Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Clarke) in bringing this Bill forward, and I should like to make a few comments on it.
The Bill under consideration proposes to make minor amendments to the Criminal Code provisions dealing with cruelty to animals. The proposal's key feature is to make a negligent act of cruelty to an animal a criminal offence. Very few negligent acts with respect to human beings are governed by the criminal law, so I do not see why we should afford more protection to animals than we do to people.
A criminal offence generally requires an actus reus and a mens rea. The act must be committed plus the person committing the act must have the required intention. Where a person does not intend the consequences of his act or does not have the necessary mental state to understand that the act is wrong, he is generally not punished by the criminal law. There are few exceptions to this rule.
The Criminal Code currently defines criminal negligence in Section 202(1). The Section states:
Everyone is criminally negligent who
(a)	in doing anything, or
(b)	in omitting to do anything that it is his duty to do,
shows wanton or reckless disregard for the lives or safety of other persons.
Subsection 202(2) adds:
For the purposes of this section, "duty" means a duty imposed by law.
This same type of recklessness is contemplated by Section 402 dealing with cruelty to animals due to the application of Section 386.
Section 386(1) provides:
Everyone who causes the occurrence of an event by doing an act or by omitting to do an act that it is his duty to do, knowing that the act or omission will probably cause the occurrence of the event and being reckless whether the event occurs or not, shall be deemed, for the purposes of this Part, wilfully to have caused the occurrence of the event.
If Section 402 is read completely and in the context of Part IX of the Code, it is apparent that advertent negligence or recklessness is already included. Further, by the operation of Subsections 402(3) and 386(1), proof of simple negligence is, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, proof of advertent negligence or recklessness.
Subsection 402(3) states:
-evidence that a person failed to exercise reasonable care or supervision of an animal or bird thereby causing it pain, suffering, damage or injury is, in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, proof that such pain, suffering, damage or injury was caused or was permitted to be caused wilfully or was caused by wilful neglect, as the case may be.
Since negligence means the failure to exercise reasonable care, the current Subsection 402(3) would appear to accomplish the intended purpose of the proposed amendment.
The Hon. Member has mentioned that the Government's policy with respect to criminal law is to reserve its use for conduct for which other means of control are inadequate and inappropriate. The Provinces have enacted legislation with respect to cruelty to animals which focuses on protection and rehabilitation of the animal rather than punishment of the owner or custodian.
The Provinces have also enacted legislation imposing certain standards of care where animals are used for research.
The current Criminal Code provisions are more than adequate to deter and punish those who deliberately or recklessly harm animals. There is no need for amendment. The proposed amendments add little to the current law.
May I also point out that it is premature to consider any amendments to the Criminal Code at this time, especially unnecessary amendments. The Members of the House of Commons are well aware that the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) is currently involved in a fundamental and comprehensive review of the Criminal Code, in the course of which Section 402 will be considered. The Criminal Code was originally enacted in 1892, and since that date there have been a continuous series of patchwork amendments. The criminal law review is aimed at the enactment of a modern, responsible and effective criminal law for Canada based on consistent and fundamental principles. This review has been undertaken in co-operation with the Ministry of the Solicitor General and in close consultation with the Provinces. The recommendations of the Law Reform Commission of Canada will be reviewed and a detailed examination of all substantive and procedural aspects of Canadian criminal law will be conducted.
Each section of the present Criminal Code will be examined in light of the principles stated in the Criminal Law in Canadian Society which were discussed by the Hon. Member. The sections will also be reviewed with regard to the numerous amendments that have been proposed but not adopted and their intended purpose.
The consideration of minor amendments to seldom used sections at this time is likely to lead to more patchwork legislation. The consideration of Section 402 will be thoroughly dealt with by the House when undertaking its analysis of proposed amendments resulting from the criminal law review process. I would therefore suggest that the proposed amendments be dealt with at that time.

Retained earnings, thus, accounted for $186.1 million of shareholder's equity at the close of 1982. The law, as it is now, creates borrowing approval for the authority of a multiple of ten times that authorized capital. This means that the corporation could today be borrowing up to $10 billion. As it stands today, the paid-in equity by the Government of Canada, indicated by the corporation itself, is $465 million, in other words, less than half the authorized capital already in the law. The borrowings of the corporation, Mr. Speaker, are less than $5 billion as compared to the authorized potential under the existing law of $10 billion.

Mr. Speaker, to answer the question put by the Hon. Member of the Opposition, I would, first of all, like to situate the report by the International Commission of Enquiry on Communications Problems and then discuss the position we took on this issue. I think the Hon. Member's picture of the report is not quite clear.
The Commission, as we all know, was created by the UNESCO General Conference in 1976. A number of experts, including one Canadian, Mrs. Betty Zimmerman, who was then Director of Radio-Canada International, were asked to sit on the Commission, which was chaired by Mr. MacBride. The Commission submitted its report in 1980 at the 21st General Conference of UNESCO in Belgrade. However, the Hon. Member ought to realize that the MacBride report was not adopted by UNESCO. Some of the recommendations it contained were the subject of a resolution adopted by consensus, inviting the Director General, Mr. M'Bow, to undertake, and I quote:
__to undertake or direct the studies and analyses required for the formulation of
concrete and practical proposals for the creation of a new world order of information and communications.
Let me reassure the Hon. Member by reminding him that the provisions of Article 14 of this Resolution list the principles on which this new order could be based. These include freedom of the press, which the Hon. Member himself already mentioned, and the article also covers the compatibility of this new order with the basic principles of international law laid down in the United Nations Charter.
Consequently, the Canadian Government does not consider the MacBride Report as authoritative as the Hon. Member seems to think it is, but takes the position that it should be seen as one of the elements of a broader body of documents on international information and communication. Canada has always had a keen interest in the problems caused by imbalances in the field of information and communications, and we are particularly aware of the importance of the problems encountered by developing countries. As an expression of this interest, we supported another resolution at the UNESCO General Conference in Belgrade, a resolution that created the International Program for the Development of Communication (IPDC), which is aimed at responding in a concrete manner to the expectations of many countries.

Adjournment Debate
The Hon. Member asked us to find out what was going on. We are in an excellent position to do so, since Canada was elected to the Intergovernmental Council of the IPDC and has taken an active part in its work. We have contributed $250,000 to the Program's operating fund. At the present time, the Program appears to be making a very valuable and highly esteemed contribution. However, 1 would like to give the Hon. Member the assurance that throughout this debate, Canada intends to defend the principles of freedom of the press and freedom of information, as we have defined them ourselves in the Canadian Constitution.

I mean that I do not regard concessionary financing as a form of foreign aid. It is a form of promotional financing offers, such as other countries make in their credit mixed packages and such as we must make if we are to sell abroad on many major projects.
Perhaps it does cost the country money in a way, but if properly handled it is the kind of public cost that should be repaid by public benefits such as an increased revenue base for Government.
All of which is to say that I could see certain kinds of arguments that the Government might have in mind as reasons for asking now to have the ceilings on EDC increased by so much. But the Government does not appear to want to grant us the courtesy of making these or any other kind of sensible arguments to convince us that the money limits it is proposing
for EDC are really needed for the corporation's exercise of its proper purposes.

What the Government appears to be proposing is that the Parliament of the people, which has grown through the centuries precisely because it has held the power of the purse strings, should step aside and allow a Crown corporation to determine, in consort with the bureaucrats of the Treasury Board and the PCO, how and when to spend a big chunk of the taxpayers' money.
This is just not acceptable. We may have the greatest respect in the world for the talents and good judgment of civil servants and Crown employees, but the fact remains that this Parliament exists, as it has always existed, to provide a check upon the Crown and its employees. The bureaucrats may have good judgment and might exercise good judgment, but when it comes to making decisions about spending public funds it is not their judgment to make. It is ours, even if we exercise judgment poorly.
It seems to me to be a fundamental principle of our parliamentary system that no funds-not even one single penny- can be properly spent without some sure and certain parliamentary authority. Merely passing a Bill that increases the statutory ceiling for EDC's capitalization does not confer any kind of spending authority at all in my view. If that is so, then the Government's apparent belief that EDC can receive new appropriations of its authorized capital merely by Order in Council and without a parliamentary appropriations Bill is wrong. Once again I say that even if we exercise bad judgment about spending public money, we here in Parliament are the only body in the land that can exercise any judgment, good or bad, about spending public money. That power to grant or to withhold money from the Crown is a power belonging to the people and held by us in trust as their elected representatives. This is not merely some vague or colourful historical theory. This is the actual fact, constitutionally recognized, and we are sworn to uphold the Constitution that recognizes it. We are also pledged, by our act of faith with our electors, to maintain for them the power to grant or withhold money from the Crown.

In Mr. Dye's opinion, over the past six years the actual progress toward better accountability has been limited, particularly as far as Parliament is concerned. In the following quote from the report this is further highlighted:
Parliament is becoming further isolated from an increasing portion of government activities. The existing legislative framework for creating, monitoring and where necessary, changing the purpose of using the corporate form for achieving public policies objectives can be abused.

Mr. Speaker,, just prior to the lunch hour adjournment, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Peterson) asked me why we chose to debate Bill C-l 10 for seven days with some 140-odd speakers. I would happily reply to that question.
Bill C-l 10, as the Parliamentary Secretary may know, was introduced in the House in May of 1981, two years and some months ago. When it was introduced into the House by the then Minister of State for Trade, he came to me as spokesman for Trade of the Conservative Party and asked me if we could very quickly dispense with the Bill. It did not seem to involve a great deal. I reviewed the Bill and agreed with him that it was not earthshaking, but I sought three amendments to the Bill. First, I wanted greater representation from the private sector on the board of directors of the Export Development Corporation. Second, I wanted the financial disclosure shown in the financial statements of the Export Development Corporation. I wanted the corporation to disclose the contingent liability with respect to the commitments the corporation had made to finance certain contracts at one rate of interest, then going out on the open market and having to finance those commitments at a higher rate of interest. Third, I wanted the Government to bring forward appropriations that were necessary to fund the Export Development Corporation from time to time. 1 wanted them brought before Parliament. The then Minister of State for Trade said; "I do not see any problem with those amendments. They seem perfectly reasonable. I think I can arrange to have those approved by my Cabinet."
Here we are, two years later, debating the Bill. They were very reasonable amendments that I put forward. We put those amendments forward in committee for over two years. We did not receive one civilized response in a period of two years to those simple, straightforward amendments, not one sign of willingness to amend the Bill in those reasonable ways. I say to the Parliamentary Secretary that that is why we were here in the House for seven days. That is why we put forth 140 speakers.

Madam Speaker, I would like to speak to this point of order. I feel that the interpretation of the Standing Order given by the Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) is exaggerated, and I can not subscribe at all to his suggestion on how to interpret the Standing Order, which in my view is quite clear and gives the Chair full discretionary powers. The fact, however, that Standing Order 79(10) gives the Chair this power and discretion does not alter the fact that according to parliamentary practice and other Standing Orders, Hon. Members are not allowed to discuss, comment on, or appeal, the rulings of the Chair. Perhaps I may remind the Chair, since I know, Madam Speaker, that you will read over the comments made by the Member for Yukon and will also take the time to read this particular Standing Order, which is quite clear, perhaps I may draw your attention to the paragraph in question which, basically, says two things: first, it gives the Speaker the power to select or combine amendments and clauses to be proposed at the report stage.
The Standing Order also gives the Speaker, and this is where the interpretation given by the Member for Yukon runs counter to the Standing Order of the House, to what this Standing Order empowers the Speaker to do, it is the power, freedom and discretion, in case of doubt, to call upon any Member who has given the Chair notice of an amendment to give such explanation of the subject of the amendment as may enable the Speaker to form a judgment upon it. There are two aspects here: the Speaker may combine or select the amendments, and once the Chair's decision is made, it cannot be discussed or appealed in the House; the second power conferred on the Speaker by Standing Order 79(10) is probably based on concern for full consideration of the matter and for ensuring that members proposing the amendments are treated in a just and equitable manner-that the Speaker is free to consult Hon. Members until the debate begins, within the period prescribed by the Standing Orders, that is, the Speaker may call upon Members and ask them for explanations, and that should be sufficient for the Chair to draw its conclusions and make a ruling, and decide whether an amendment is acceptable or not.
27542

September 28, 1983
Business of the House
As for suggesting that the Chair reverse its ruling because, with or without consultation, it had decided that an amendment was unacceptable, as for raising a point of order and having a debate on each amendment or several or a few or only one, I submit this goes against parliamentary practice, because Hon. Members may not appeal a ruling by the Chair, and the Standing Order is quite clear, and empowers the Speaker, and I quote:
-to form a judgment upon the subject of the amendment.
Once the Chair has formed a judgment, it can no longer be discussed, and we intend to respect the Standing Order. I do not agree at all with the interpretation given by my learned colleague from Yukon. In fact, I think he is giving us notice of a procedural debate that could take weeks and months-it is very easy to paralyze Parliament. The equity he is seeking, and the concern-if he is sincere, and 1 do not doubt that he is-he seems to have that each amendment, even if there are a great many, be given serious consideration, all that is covered by the Standing Order. With due respect, I submit that the Chair must consider the amendments within the limits prescribed by the Standing Order and not according to the interpretation preferred by a Member of the Opposition. In other words, if the Chair has any doubts, it can consult with any Member of this House, but once the Chair has formed a judgment, I submit that we should not waste any more of the time of the House on discussing that judgment. We have no right to discuss it. In the circumstances, I submit that we should apply Standing Order 79(10) very strictly. That is the appropriate procedure, contained in the Standing Orders of the House of Commons of Canada.

This particular amendment is an attempt to get the voice of labour on this particular Committee. The Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) defends western farmers and this particular Bill. He has spent a considerable amount of time attempting to impute a feeling to the New Democratic Party that this particular Committee will not do any good. We know that the Committee has some flaws and that the Bill has some flaws. We also know that the total direction of this Bill as far as farmers are concerned is to reduce effectively the possibility of their survival.
Since we have the Bill before us and it seems that the Government is foolhardy enough to eliminate its chances in the West by passing the Bill or keeping it before the House, we must make it the best Bill possible. One way to make the committee work well is not, as the Hon. Member for Vegreville suggested, by eliminating any particular group, such as the co-operatives. We should bring in as many of them as possible. We made a motion to add labour to the regular Committee. This particular approach was turned down not only by the Liberals but by the Conservatives. We now allow labour at least to have an observer status. When one can only have the crumbs, I guess one accepts them. We need a strong labour voice. By having a labour member as an observer, at least there will be somebody there able to put forward labour's case.
In the last few years there have been a couple of grain handler strikes. Actually there have been very few. There are so many unions involved in the movement of grain that if one
Western Grain Transportation Act
of them strikes, it affects the whole operation. We need someone on the committee who can present the views of labour. It could work both ways. Having a labour representative will help to get out the story of labour a little better and to a few more people than would be the case with no representative on the Committee. Also labour will be able to understand a little better the position of farmers.
Every time there is a strike in the grain handling system, there is a great movement across the country to do something about the labour union. I am a farmer. 1 know that the movement of grain is important, but 1 think the time has come when we have to look at who pays the penalty for a strike. When there is a strike in the grain handling system, farmers are affected by the possibility that their grain will not be sold as quickly as it would have. Eventually they will be able to sell their grain, but they may have to carry it over a few weeks or months longer. If affects them because they are paying interest on money and it stops their cash flow. It also' affects the labourers, those working in every facet of the grain-moving operation. They are the ones to go without wages for the period of time the union is on strike.
In addition, a large number of elevators are involved in grain handling. They are paid for this handling of grain. Whether they handle it now or later does not make much difference as they will still be paid. When the grain is not moving, they are paid for storing it. Therefore, even while the unions are on strike the grain elevator companies including to co-ops go on collecting the storage charges. The grain handling strike does not affect the elevator companies. They are not affected the same way as the farmers, and obviously the union members who go without wages.
It is time the House looked at the penalties consequent upon a strike. There are two sides to every strike. If only labour pays the penalty, the grain companies collect storage charges as well as handling the grain later, whether this week, next week or two weeks down the road, they do not have much to lose. It is time that Parliament looked at imposing some kind of penalty on the other people involved in a strike.
Labour has made concessions to make the movement of grain more smooth over the years. If labour can be more knowledgeable about the needs of the system, I am sure we can find some kind of arrangement whereby labour will not always be on the outside. The Leader of the Opposition does not think that we should "Swedenize" industry in Canada. 1 say to him that "Swedenizing" must be pretty good because Swedish industry has fewer days lost to strikes than any other country. Labour is part of the discussion on every development in Sweden. That is what we should have here.

(1)	that the question raised thereby had already been decided by the committee;

They would rather not enter into agreements that would benefit the farmers if those trains were taken off their own lines. Therefore, it made common sense to us that if additional taxpayer dollars are to be put at the disposal of the railroads, they would have to accept the responsibility under legislation to maximize the returns to the producers.
