Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the intent of our amendment with regard to providing for an acceptable ratio of ward versus private and semi-private beds in hospitals is to ensure that the overall goals of the Canada Health Act are indeed achieved throughout the country. One of our concerns is that if this is not specified in the Bill it is possible that a two-tier hospital care system could develop.
We have seen, particularly since 1977, and more specifically in the last couple of years, a trend on the part of certain provincial governments to encourage hospitals to find ways of generating revenue on their own. One way to achieve that, of course, is by turning more of their bed capacity over to the classification of private or semi-private rooms so that they generate revenue over and above that which would be generated through ordinary ward beds under the health insurance plan.
We wanted to ensure that this Act would provide a mandate to the Minister of National Health and Welfare to take action, should she or he in the future discern that a province is evading universality and accessibility, with respect to clause 12, by not making a suitable number of beds available under the plan. This is not a new idea and has been done before by regulation. We feel this should be made explicit in the Canada Health Act. If this is not done, a situation could arise where accessibility could be threatened by a lack of availability of ward beds. This would then create a situation in which Canadians would rightly want to insure themselves against the unavailability of those beds, if it were seen as something that is inevitable. Eventually Canadians would feel that they have to take out private health insurance to make sure that they could get a bed when they needed it because the hospitals in their area were following that kind of policy. Very soon, the very thing we are trying to prevent in this Bill, through elimination of extra billing and user fees, could take place with respect to the availability of beds. Therefore, this amendment seems to be self-evidently in keeping with the spirit of the Canada Health Act.
I did not see any reason in committee and I do not see any reason now why this amendment cannot be enshrined in the Bill.
The amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Oxford is a reintroduction of an amendment many of us tried to move in committee in various forms which would meet what I consider to be the very legitimate concerns of the Canadian
Association of Interns and Residents, which is that all people who graduate from medicine and are licensed to practice medicine should be able to do so in the plan wherever they so choose, so long as they want to meet the conditions of the plan.
I am not saying doctors who want to extra-bill in a province where extra billing has been outlawed should be able to operate within the plan. That is not the kind of right we are talking about. We are talking about the right of physicians to have geographical freedom within a particular province. This Bill is directed at what is going on in British Columbia and what could go on in many other provinces where we find provincial governments, through the limitation of billing numbers per area, restricting the right of physicians to practise in a particular area. I think this is something that should be addressed in another way. If provinces want to find ways of redistributing physician manpower, then there must be a way that is more acceptable than refusing the right to practise in this way, particularly when you consider that there are people now graduating from our medical colleges who are now interns and residents and who, if they want to practise in B.C., for instance, face the possibility of not being able to do so. Also, as was pointed out to me by people concerned, there is one case where a husband got a billing number and the wife did not. The wife is also a physician. The only way she could practise medicine was to move away from where her husband was living and practise somewhere else. That is completely unacceptable. We have an opportunity to do something about that in this Bill. This amendment is the result of many, many refinements. I see no reason, nor, I am sure, does the Hon. Member for Oxford why we could not meet in the Bill those very legitimate concerns of the Canadian Association of Interns and Residents.

Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) I was somewhat surprised, after the hours of committee deliberations, to hear and read that there was not much controversy and not much input by the opposition Parties to the application of Bill C-3, the amendments now coming out of it, and those that were considered in committee. Yet, through a devious and roundabout way, they are being affected by Bill C-3, which may affect medicare, in a way we may not have properly and thoroughly considered.

However, the Government does not see it that way because it has a fixation on the two potential erosionary capacities of user fees and extra billing. BasePK: 3471461

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, in his question of March 21 concerning the costs of Canada Lands exploration, the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) referred to expenditures of taxpayers' dollars on high-risk exploration in the amount of $12 billion by 1986. For the record, I would like to point out that the forecast of expenditure under the Petroleum Incentives Program for the period January 1, 1981 to the end of 1986 is $8 billion on all lands in Canada. This includes payments under the program for Alberta, financed by the government of that province, which, together with Petroleum Incentives Program payments for programs in other provinces, account for close to 30 per cent of the total program. Consequently, Canada Lands exploration will receive something in the order of $5.6 billion over the period 1981-1986, not $12 billion. There will be an equal distribution of the $5.6 billion between Canada Lands in the north and off the East Coast.
March 26, 1984

Turning to the Hon. Member's objective of generating thousands of jobs through oil sands development, the primary purpose of oil exploration and development is to open up the country's oil resource potential for present and future generations. The extent to which this primary objective generates jobs is a very welcome consequence and, in this connection, Canada Lands exploration is producing jobs in areas where they are badly needed, particularly in the Atlantic provinces.
The argument is sometimes made that we should put all of our effort into the oil sands because the oil is there and the technology is known. The fact is that oil sands development is not without its risks and, in the matter of technology, reference could be made to a recently published statement by C. W. Bowman, head of the Alberta Oil Sands Technology and Research Authority, who said: "-in spite of progress to date, further quantum jumps in technology will be required before the full impact of the oil sands is realized".
The policy of this Government is to proceed on all fronts in working toward the objective of oil self-sufficiency. The results off the Newfoundland and Nova Scotia coasts have demonstrated the value of this approach.
At the same time, federal policy is very actively directed to oil sands and heavy oil development. The federal Government operates major incentives for the opening up of these resources including the provision of earned depletion allowance, relief from the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax, the world oil price, and special provisions to encourage heavy oil processing and marketing. The fact that the Cold Lake, Wolf Lake, and Elk Point oil sands projects are underway is evidence of the effectiveness of these measures, and of the royalty reduction provisions of the provinces. Other similar projects will not be long in coming.
In these brief comments, Mr. Speaker, I have emphasized the importance of an integrated program of oil resource development. Results show that it is paying off in terms of new resources while at the same time generating economic benefits for regions most in need.

Medical care is no place for any kind of means test. No matter how prudent a citizen is in this country, he or she can never predict the seriousness or length of illness or illness resulting from accidents that might happen.

Mr. Speaker, the federal Government fully supports the volunteer movement in Canada and recognizes

April 9, 1984
Adjournment Debate
the important role it plays in providing or supplementing various services in the community. The question of volunteer service has become an important issue, and many advocate the use of the income tax system to provide incentives to encourage volunteer services in Canada. However, the effectiveness of the tax system depends upon its integrity and fairness.
Contributions of money and time in volunteer service is basically personal and undertaken at a taxpayer's discretion. The related expenses of providing the service are therefore personal expenses. Because of the possibility of the misdirection of tax incentives for personal gains, tax concessions are not generally provided in respect of personal expenses, even when they are expended to earn income; for example the cost of transportation to and from work. Given this general tax principle, it would be very difficult to introduce tax benefits for volunteer services which would be fair to the taxpaying public who must ultimately finance these benefits.
An exception has already been provided in the Income Tax Act by way of the $500 exemption in respect of allowances received by volunteer firemen from a government, municipality or other public authority. This exemption is in addition to the 20 per cent employement expense deduction, to a maximum of $500, available to all employees including volunteer firemen.
The $500 exemption differs from the provision which is proposed in that under current law the authority which grants the allowance serves as an independent control to ensure that the expenses incurred are reasonable and valid. Permitting a deduction of these expenses would clearly increase the administrative cost of ensuring that expenses are reasonable. It would also further aggravate the disparity between volunteer firemen and other volunteer workers, such as St. John's Ambulance drivers who constantly point out the inequity of a tax concession for firemen with no similar treatment for themselves.
At this time of budgetary constraint it would be difficult to justify to the tax-paying public further exemptions. This is so especially in light of the fact that the responsibility for providing municipal services, such as protection against fire, is not properly the responsibility of the federal Government, but that of local and provincial governments.

Mr. Speaker, during the Second United Nations Special Session on Disarmament in 1982, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) drew attention to the urgency of coming to grips with the development of new weaponry for use in outer space. He noted how quickly in today's world science fiction had become reality and how inadequate the Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space had become. There were loopholes in the Treaty which risked being highly destabilizing. He had in mind particularly anti-satellite weapons or anti-missile laser systems. As he pointed out then, "we cannot wait much longer if we are to be successful in foreclosing the prospect of space wars". He therefore proposed that an early start be made on a treaty to prohibit the development, testing and deployment of all weapons for use in outer space.
In the Committee on Disarmament in Geneva, now called the Conference on Disarmament, we have been working for the establishment of a working group to discuss outer space issues, including an anti-satellite treaty. We were close to reaching an agreement on setting up such a body at the 1983 session of the Conference on Disarmament, but the Soviet Union required time to refer the matter to Moscow. So far during the current session of the CD no agreement has been reached on this working group.
It is not surprising, in light of what I have already said, that in developing his initiative the Prime Minister focused on the question of outer space, and particularly anti-satellite weapons. We were aware that for some years the Soviet Union had been testing an anti-satellite system directed at low-flying satellites. By the beginning of this year the U.S.A. had also tested a comparable system. Neither superpower, however, has

April 10, 1984
Adjournment Debate
yet developed an anti-satellite system for high altitudes. It was our belief that an agreement not to do so was therefore still possible.
As part of his initiative, the Prime Minister proposed a ban on the testing and deployment of those anti-satellite systems designed to operate at high altitudes where the race has not yet begun. It was our view that such systems, by attacking global communications satellites which are located in high altitudes and which are of critical importance for crisis management, could be particularly destabilizing. It would leave an adversary blind and mute at the very moment when stability demands awareness and response. We are continuing our consultations with our NATO allies on this proposal.
Outer space is a subject to which we have been devoted and are continuing to devote a great deal of attention. Our whole approach to this question is governed by our concern about the possible militarization of outer space and its destabilizing effect on superpower relationships.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to join in this debate today to share the concerns of many of my colleagues about what we are debating today and to talk about the insensitivity and disregard of the Government for the agricultural sector of the country. This is not a very nice subject to have to talk about. The fact that we must remind the Government of its responsibility to an industry which overall employs about 18 per cent of the labour force, represents about 40 per cent of Canada's economy, accounts for 10 per cent of our exports, and generates $7 for every SI spent, is, simply put, appalling.
While the Government appears to be willing to provide money, incentives such as rebates, tax credits and so on in large amounts to so many other sectors, it is completely unwilling to respond in a positive way to the demands of agriculture. When a positive step is taken, it is generally only as a result of years of complaint from the farmers themselves and from this side of the House. The Government appears to be unwilling to take the initiative to place agriculture high enough on its list of priorities. This is the root of the problem.
The biggest crisis is the unavailability of affordable credit. Interest rates now appear to be on the rise again; we are seeing that every day. We have just come out of a period of very high interest rates. They were as high as 21.24 per cent in August of 1981 and even higher for some first mortgages. According to the Conference Board of Canada, continuing high levels of interest rates are going to be one of the major factors in a projected slow down in the economy. This is occurring at a
Supply
time when farmers can least afford an increase in the rates of credit. Unlike other sectors, agriculture is still hurting from the recent recession. Last year farm bankruptcies were up 16 per cent from 1982; they rose from 410 to 488. Ontario let the nation with a total of 165 declared bankruptcies. There were probably as many or even more, undeclared bankruptcies. Prairie farm failures doubled last year. By the end of February this year farm bankruptcies were up 58 per cent over the same period last year.
The main point that must be made, Mr. Speaker, is that farmers are still hurting very badly. They have not seen this recovery of which the Liberals boast. A very well respected financial constultant was quoted recently in the London Free Press as saying that many farmers continue to suffer the painful hangover of recession. Some may never get over it. If interest rates rise now many will be forced into the red and off the farm. He estimates about 40 per cent of farmers are in financial difficulty. If banks and governments keep hiding their heads in the sand, no solution is possible for farmers.
The outlook for farmers is not good, Mr. Speaker. Debt loads carried by agriculture will soon reach $20 billion. Farm input costs are high and have increased at a much higher rate than prices which farmers receive for their products. Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. I will try to answer it in two parts. One is the concern we have about the proposed method of appointment, and then I will try to answer directly his question about what we believe would be better.
There is always a concern in terms of the Cabinet when by Order in Council appointments may be seen to be or may in fact be not as non-partisan as they should be. On this issue we do not believe it is. What we believe ought to be done and what we should look for is a method whereby the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence could be asked to make appointments to the board on the understanding that the Committee had to operate on a consensus basis and not on a simple majority vote basis. We believe that out of the process of coming to agreement would come non-partisan appointments.
That is the process we believe should be used to make these appointments. The Hon. Member may ask whether Parliament could do that. I know of no mechanism that allows Parliament to do that as a whole. That is why I think we believe the committee should have that power.

CEIC officials are to meet with union representatives to seek their support for this committee. Speech:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the use of weapons in space, let me say first that I am of the opinion that technological progress in regard to the use of space both for military and peaceful purposes cannot be stopped. It will go ahead irrespective of what is said in this Parliament or in almost any congress or parliament. I have tended to touch on that matter in several speeches I have made in the House. The question in my mind is the deployment of the deadly device
April 18, 1984

itself, the nuclear weapon. There are now 50,000 in the world. We have to return to the question of reducing the number.
The danger is not with the development of technology because all technology that is developed, whether it is the jeep or the initial airplane, can be used for destruction or construction. Indeed, we have gone through several systems in which the initial development was for military purposes but then they have been used massively for commercial or peaceful purposes.
I cannot think of any single development in technology that has not gone through this variation from possible military use to usefulness in society. I suggest that we must deal with reducing the number of nuclear bombs themselves.
One of the most interesting aspects, of course, is Canada's position in regard to the CANDU nuclear reactor. Canada is trying to market nuclear reactors all over the world in a very significant fashion. I know quite a bit about CANDU reactors because I have worked on the design of some. Yet this is a reactor that we sell which makes it possible to build a nuclear bomb without too much difficulty. We must examine closely our position in regard to the development of technology. I am not suggesting that we should not sell CANDU reactors. That is my answer to the first question.
With respect to the second question regarding the testing of nuclear Cruise missiles, I have stated my position in the House very emphatically. I think I was the first person in the House to take a position in respect of testing the Cruise missile. It was that we should go ahead. To support that view, I return to the process of verifiability and the timeframe for delivery systems. The Cruise missile is a slow delivery system. I feel rather safe with the Cruise missile, as I feel with an airplane, because I believe that nuclear war can start by design, which is first strike capability, if you wish; by escalation as a result of initiation by a small country, such as one in the Middle East; or by accident. I do not fear the first alternative at all. I know of no nation that will start a nuclear war knowing that it will accelerate very rapidly and will not stop until the world is destroyed.
I fear the second instance, of a bomb dropped in Israel, the Middle East, or somewhere else, which act of aggression would then escalate. But I mostly fear the third alternative. I am a technologist. I have worked on nuclear reactors and I know how accidents can happen. My fear is that the Cruise missile has a slow delivery. We have time to react. It is verifiable-not the Cruise missile itself but the bomb itself when it is stationed at some particular point. The bomb is verifiable. A nuclear bomb when it is stationed somewhere brings around it a massive system of protection against somebody stealing it. There is no harm in stealing a Cruise missile. The harm is in stealing the bomb. It is the bomb that will provide the verifiability with respect to the protection systems around it. With respect to the Cruise missile, it is slow. It will give us time to react and stop any escalation process. Second, the nuclear bomb itself and its location is a verifiable process.

BasePK: 3477687

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the time has come when all large hospitals and medical schools must have a formal ethics committee. With the current rapid social transformation, and with the continuing advances in medical technology and techniques, doctors and society at large face dilemmas beyond the imagination of other generations.
It is not enough, as is the custom now, for complex ethical decisions to be made at a meeting of the medical advisory board of a hospital, or by a special committee struck for a specific issue. A formal ethics committee in a hospital must consist of medical staff, social workers, religious representatives, and legal advisers. Less formal committees are more ideal in difficult situations such as making a decision as to whether or not to discontinue life support systems and should, therefore, involve only people most closely involved with the patient-the family, the doctor, and the religious adviser.
These groups in their discussions need the expertise of a person trained to deal with the ethical question, that is, an ethicist. Such people may come from a variety of professions, medicine, law, philosophy or theology. At least one year's intense training is desirable to prepare such individuals. There are only a handful of such persons at the moment in Canada. As an important matter of concern, I feel that financial support from the Government is the stimulus which is required to encourage and promote the establishment of the essential services of ethicists throughout our country.

Section 16 of the Interpretation Act says, in effect, that a statute is binding on the Crown only if the statute expressly says it is binding on the Crown. This is very important when we consider the lessons of history. Hon. Members will recall that the Ontario and Supreme Courts recently held that the federal Combines Investigation Act did not bind the Crown in the form of Eldorado Nuclear Limited and Uranium Canada Incorporated in the so-called "Uranium Cartel" case, which is a national scandal. The purpose of a second reading stage debate in our parliamentary lexicon is to determine whether or not the principles embodied in a Bill are worthy of the support of the people who represent the electors in this country in the Parliament of Canada.

Of course, it is a fairly new Crown corporation which came into being mid-way through the 1970s. That Crown corporation is called Petro-Canada. It has had many subsidiaries that have grown like Topsy since it was initially formed.
Has that Crown corporation created a problem? I had never run for public office and was not a member of the Chamber when Petro-Canada was formed. I was merely a member of the community. I am sure Hon. Members will recognize that the oil and gas industry is important to the City of Calgary because it is a major employer and a prime source of economic health to that community. We have also discovered recently that it can be a major source of economic disaster.

The first thing that corporation did was to hire employees from the marketplace. It was willing to pay 30 per cent to 40 per cent more than the marketplace was paying people at that time. This meant that it immediately distorted the marketplace and created, in effect, runaway inflation in salaries. In turn, this affected all of those companies that were previously in existence. The multinational and large corporations were able to compete because of the residual economic power they had, but it created enormous difficulties for small Canadian operators. That was the first effect of this Crown corporation.
Being a Crown corporation, it was subject to the laws of Parliament and the control of Cabinet. It operated in an industry that characteristically was mainly composed of what I would call peculiar people. I suggest that peculiar people are needed to meet the aspirations of such an industry. What we have in terms of the engineers and geologists who guide us in exploration work is a group of people who go to university for many years and obtain many years of experience, are willing to sit in the bush in temperatures of 30 and 40 degrees below zero for many days. They do this to help the country achieve self-sufficiency in oil and gas. I think that is peculiar. But those peculiar people are extremely skilled and very independent. They are special people in this country who are out in the field having to make life and death decisions instantly. They are responsible for millions of dollars of shareholders' money in the drilling of those wells. They have a particular temperament and philosophy and are willing to work 24 hours a day.
All of those are characteristics that do not hold well for employment by the Government in the bureaucracy. Nevertheless, the Liberal Government of the day decided to form that Crown corporation. It is now 1984. What do Calgarians see when they look at the Calgary skyline? They see the tallest building in town which has a red stone exterior. That tallest building is the PetroCan tower. It is a Crown corporation tower.
What does one find when one enters the front doors of that building? One finds that floor after floor of that immense tower are closed. One only sees emptiness because no one is working there.

Normally producers contribute 2 per cent of the value of their grain sales and the Government of Canada contributes an additional 4 per cent. This money is deposited in an interest bearing account, the western grain stabilization fund, for use when prairie grain incomes are depressed.
Because of the actuarial mechanism, contributions were reduced on January 1, 1984 to 1.5 per cent for producers and 3.5 per cent for the Government in light of large fund balances. Proportionately, therefore, producers have benefited more from this, with a 25 per cent reduction, then has the Government, with a 12.5 per cent reduction.
Pay-outs under the original Western Grain Stabilization Act are triggered when net cash flow, which is essentially receipts less cash costs, fall below the previous five year average. Despite lower grain prices over the past two years, total receipts have not fallen because volumes sold have been increasing so that pay-outs have not been triggered.
The intention of the Western Grain Stabilization Act was to have an actuarially sound producer-contributory program. Even in its proposed amended form, it is important to note that the actuarial soundness will be preserved. It would be imprudent to amend the Act in such a way as to undermine its actuarial mechanism, as would be the case if all producer contributions to date were simply reimbursed. This could seriously deplete the fund, leaving inadequate amounts available in case pay-outs are triggered next year or beyond.
The Government intends, however, to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act to make it more responsive to the needs of the prairie grain economy. Under the proposed payout mechanism, participating producers will receive larger and earlier payouts than the existing Act would provide. The actuarial soundness of the program will, however, be maintained so that the funds will continue to be managed in a responsible manner.

Mr. Speaker, at first blush the motion seems rather appealing to parliamentarians. Given a quick reading, one would think the motion would expand the role of Parliament in expenditure control and increase the level of accountability, which is of course a buzzword for Members of Parliament. After all, keeping the Government accountable is the raison d'etre of Parliament. Parliament is a talking shop, but the debate has to have a point. The purpose of our debate is to ensure that the programs we approve are well directed; that the policy thrust is sound; and that the targeting of programs is accurate. What I mean by that is that we must ensure that the money we appropriate goes to where it is needed most. Once these programs are in place, Mr. Speaker, it is Parliament's task to see that they continue to be implemented in the way approved by Parliament; that they do not become diverted; that the programs do not in some way change course and go beyond the spirit and will of Parliament.
The task of program evaluation is a difficult one to impose upon politicians. If that were our task, even in the enlarged and expanded committee proposed by the Hon. Member, then we would need a great deal of expert help in program evaluation. That is my difficulty with the motion. I see it as being somewhat too narrow in its scope. It is primarily concerned with the amounts expended. However, if we are talking about accountability in all its aspects, it means ensuring that the programs on which funds are expended continue to meet the Government's priorities and objectives as approved by Parliament.
Government Expenditure
For a long while now the Government of Canada has recognized the importance of its own internal accountability system. The Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) quite rightly drew attention to this system. The people of Canada should know that there is and has been developing within the Government of Canada quite an admirable program evaluation system. It has been on going since the 1960s. It has been improved upon ever since. For example, we now have the Office of the Comptroller General. We now have the policy and expenditure management system, known as PEMS. We have Estimates now which are much easier to work with. They are more enlightening for parliamentarians working in committee and examining them. The Treasury Board has provided resources in all Departments for this evaluation activity to go on. While this activity goes on, there can be adjustments and corrections as required. The Auditor General, himself a servant of Parliament, has been interested in this entire process. He calls it "measuring cost-effectiveness".
These evaluation activities in government were not always as satisfactory as they are today. Today there is a requirement in every Department of government to evaluate not just the new programs which come into effect but all programs on a regular three-year to five-year cycle. They must show that moneys spent are applied efficiently and effectively in pursuit of the objectives of the Government as approved by Parliament. The oversight of all this activity is of course carried out by the Comptroller General whom I mentioned earlier.
I would like to review very quickly what this program evaluation system requires of each Department. There are three requirements: first, a need for programs in terms of the current, social and economic environment and current government priorities must be examined; second, an actual performance of the program in achieving desired objectives; and third, a potential for enhancing the cost effectiveness of programs through redesigned and improved operations, in other words, to upgrade efficiency.
Lest it be thought in this House or in the country at large that the program evaluation process, which has been improving all along, is still not very effective, let me remind Hon. Members that very recently a former Comptroller General, Mr. Harry Rogers, received recognition for his excellent work in that office in the area of program evaluation. In 1983, he was the recipient of the Myrdal Award for Government from the International Evaluation Research Society. A growing number of other government officials have been coming to Canada to see what we are doing. They have been impressed, and we have received a good deal of recognition.

Mr. Speaker, I have a sense of deja vu when I rise to speak on this day on this issue. I have spoken about this so many times that it becomes perhaps boring and certainly repetitious. It is, I think, the single most important question that faces us in Canada at the moment. It is the cause of much of our economic difficulty. In part, if not in whole, it is the reason why we have such high levels of unemployment. It has been the Achilles' heel of our farming community. It has resulted in bankruptcies of small business the likes of which we have not seen in this century. It has played havoc with the dreams of many people and families as they attempt to plan their future as best they can.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) says that having high interest rates is not the policy of the Government. I have heard that phrase on numerous occasions over the course of the last four years. The Government's policy may not be to have high interest rates, but it certainly has inflicted high interest rates on the people of Canada.
Everyone says that high interest rates are a result of the policy set by the administration in the United States. Listening to the debate, you feel that there is nothing we can do about it, that it is our lot to suffer from that policy, that as an independent nation there is very little if anything from a
legislative or economic point of view that we in Canada can actually embark upon that will in any way assist us. High interest rates in Canada have followed to a large extent the movement of interest rates in the United States. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), quite rightly said that our interest rates no longer follow those in the United States but in fact lead them. For some time they have led interest rates in the United States. Interest rates have been the main vehicle used by this Liberal Government to strengthen or at least stabilize the value of the dollar over the United States currency.
Every time we raise the question, we are confronted with the same answer: "There is nothing we can do about it". Frankly, I do not accept that. Although I recognize that any actions that we might take would be difficult and although I recognize that any actions we might take would have certain repercussions, the policy that we are now following is difficult and has repercussions. The one thing that I know for certain is that whatever the consequence of our actions, if we want to take actions to lower interest rates, they could not possibly result in more chaos or hardship for Canadian families than the policy being pursued by the Government today of following lock-step behind the United States administration.
This is not an anti-U.S. speech I am making. I want to make that quite clear. Frankly, I do not much care what economic policy the United States follows within the United States. I do not think it is much of my business what policy the United States administration decides to pursue in what it deems to be its own best interests. However, I do care when we in Canada do not have either the will or the desire to attempt to establish for ourselves an independent path that will result in some form of autonomy, in a fiscal and economic sense, for Canada in the future.
If we are going to pursue lock-step the policies of the United States, we are doomed to face these situations over and over again. If we are to tie our interest rates and therefore tie our economy, job creation, ability to house our nation, ability to deal with the question of financing for our small businesses and farming community, if we are to tie all of that to decisions of the United States at every single turn, the consequence can be nothing other than that if they manage their economy badly, we suffer, and if we make the wrong decisions, we suffer. That is unacceptable. I did not get elected to Parliament in order to accept without question the direction being thrust upon us by the United States. Neither did I get elected in order to try to satisfy the demand of the United States for additional capital year after year, as will no doubt be the case in years to come.
I know as I stand here that the people of Canada would be prepared, if need be, to take and hold certain consequences to themselves in the short run if they were assured that the Government had a program which would divorce us economically, to the extent that that is possible, from the fluctuations that continue to occur within the United States as a result of an administration gone wild.
